claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element automotive alloy containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios.
An atomically dispersed minor dopant will stabilize active catalytic sites under transient and low-temperature exhaust conditions.
Dopant incorporation will mitigate activity loss and durability limitations.
The dopant intervention will maintain low platinum-group-metal consumption.
A single lanthanide or selected transition-metal dopant can be introduced uniformly across the catalyst surface.
A new machine-learning computational method can optimize the dopant's identity, composition, and placement.
The atomically dispersed dopant will preferentially segregate to catalytically active sites.
Dopant segregation to active sites will prevent catalyst sintering.
Dopant segregation to active sites will prevent the formation of inactive phases.
The dopant will alter catalyst surface energetics.
Altered surface energetics will reduce phase segregation and sintering during stress conditions.
Computationally guided dopant selection and concentration will maintain catalytic activity without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the doped catalyst will show improved activity retention under transient, low-temperature, wet, NO-containing, and aged conditions.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the doped catalyst will show improved durability over time.
The doped catalyst will use a similarly low amount of platinum-group metals as the untreated catalyst.
The hypothesis applies only when synthesis permits uniform dopant incorporation.
The intervention may fail when operating conditions exceed the dopant's stabilization capability or induce irreversible phase transformations.
